title: JESUS SAID THE EVIL YOU FEAR IS CLOSER THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs:
JESUS SAID THE EVIL YOU FEAR IS CLOSER THAN YOU THINK
What Christ Meant When He Said Evil Comes From Within the Heart—and Why the Most Frightening Sinner You Will Ever Have to Face May Be the One Looking Back at You in the Mirror
There is something Jesus said that destroys one of the most comforting lies we tell ourselves.
It is the lie that evil is mostly “out there.”
In people whose sins happen to be more visible than ours.
We look at someone who destroyed a marriage and think, I would never do that.
We hear about someone caught stealing and think, What kind of person does something like that?
We watch another Christian fall publicly and quietly wonder how someone who claimed to love God could become capable of such hypocrisy.
And somewhere beneath all that disappointment can hide a dangerous little assumption:
And suddenly there is nowhere left to hide.
Because Christ does not merely point toward the darkness surrounding humanity.
He points toward something inside humanity.
“From within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts…”
The Greek is even more arresting:
ἔσωθεν γὰρ ἐκ τῆς καρδίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων
esōthen gar ek tēs kardias tōn anthrōpōn
“For from within, out of the heart of human beings…”
That word ἔσωθεν — esōthen means “from within,” “from the inside.”
And καρδία — kardia, “heart,” is not merely the organ beating inside your chest, nor is it simply the modern idea of your emotions.
In biblical thought, the heart describes the inner person—the center from which desires, intentions, thoughts, commitments, and moral decisions emerge.
And He did not allow us to remain spectators.
He put every human heart on the operating table.
That is what makes Mark 7 so uncomfortable.
Jesus had been confronted over ritual purity. His disciples were being criticized because they ate without following the traditional ceremonial handwashing practices of the elders.
But Jesus drove the conversation somewhere much deeper.
He essentially forced His hearers to confront a question far more frightening than, “What touched me?”
Jesus said what enters a person from outside does not enter the heart but the stomach. Then He delivered the diagnosis:
“What comes out of a person is what defiles him.”
Not a list designed to make religious people feel superior.
διαλογισμοὶ οἱ κακοί — dialogismoi hoi kakoi
“All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.”
Jesus did not say every person commits every conceivable evil act.
He did not say temptation itself is identical to committing sin.
He did not teach that every intrusive or unwanted thought makes someone guilty of carrying out the evil it depicts.
And He certainly was not giving Christians permission to look at suffering people and accuse them of secretly wanting every darkness that crosses their minds.
Humanity's fundamental moral problem cannot be solved merely by controlling the environment around us because sin is not merely an environmental contamination.
Something has gone wrong within us.
Because we are remarkably talented at blaming what is outside.
“I became angry because of what she said.”
“I lied because I was under pressure.”
“I looked because it appeared on my screen.”
“I became bitter because they hurt me.”
“I cheated because my marriage was already falling apart.”
“I gossip because what I said was true.”
“I became obsessed with money because I need security.”
“I haven't forgiven because they don't deserve forgiveness.”
And sometimes the wounds behind those sentences are painfully real.
Jesus never requires us to call evil good.
But there is a difference between explaining the circumstances in which sin surfaced and identifying the source from which sin came.
Pressure can reveal something without creating it.
The pressure explains why the contents appeared at that moment.
But the pressure did not manufacture the contents.
That is why some of the most revealing moments of your spiritual life may be the moments you wish everyone would forget.
The argument when something vicious came out of your mouth.
The private browser history nobody knows exists.
The jealousy you felt when your friend's prayer was answered before yours.
The strange satisfaction when someone who hurt you finally suffered.
The lie that escaped almost effortlessly.
The resentment you rehearse while smiling politely.
The spiritual pride that whispers, At least I'm not like them.
Those moments can be terrifying because sometimes what shocks us most is not what somebody did to us.
It is what came out of us afterward.
Have you ever said something in anger and five minutes later wondered:
Jesus answered that question two thousand years ago.
That does not mean circumstances are irrelevant.
It means circumstances are insufficient as an explanation for our moral condition.
And here is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere behavior management.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better.
He came because sinners need something far deeper than improved appearances.
The Old Testament had already prepared us for this diagnosis.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?”
The Hebrew word translated “heart” is לֵב — lev, a word frequently referring to the inner person—the seat of thought, will, desire, and moral orientation.
Centuries before Jesus stood before that crowd, God had already promised through Ezekiel something astonishing:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you…”
Notice the location of God's promised work.
This is where the story becomes breathtaking.
Because the One exposing the human heart is the very One who came to save human beings.
The Physician giving the diagnosis came carrying the cure.
Christianity does not say, “Your heart has darkness in it, so make yourself worthy enough for God.”
That would leave every one of us condemned.
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
God knows exactly what is inside you.
He knows the thought you would be horrified to have projected onto a screen.
He knows the bitterness underneath your worship songs.
He knows how much of your generosity secretly wants recognition.
He knows the jealousy beneath the congratulations.
He knows the pride hidden inside your theology.
He knows the difference between the person everyone applauds and the person who exists when nobody is watching.
There has never been a moment when Jesus was deceived about you.
And still He went to the cross.
We spend enormous energy editing ourselves for human approval.
Jesus walked straight past the edited version.
And rather than pretending our corruption wasn't serious, He went to Calvary because it was.
The cross simultaneously destroys two lies.
My sin isn't really that bad.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required the saving work of Christ.
But the cross destroys another lie too:
My sin is so bad that Jesus could never want me.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is finally agreeing with God about what has been killing you.
It is laying down the exhausting defense.
No more polishing the outside while starving the inside.
No more pretending the pornography is harmless.
No more baptizing greed as ambition.
No more disguising unforgiveness as discernment.
No more performing holiness while secretly feeding what crucified your Savior.
And that confession can feel terrifying.
Until you remember who is standing in front of you.
The One who did not merely come to expose sinners but to redeem them.
Scripture says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not repair yourself enough to deserve mercy.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Grace did not rename persecution as an innocent mistake.
Christ transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The Gospel never needs to make sin smaller in order to make grace beautiful.
Grace is beautiful precisely because our sin is real and Christ is sufficient.
Maybe that is why this teaching of Jesus feels so personal.
Because somewhere inside you there may be a room you keep locked.
You tell everyone you are okay.
But there is a door inside your heart you hope Jesus never opens.
Maybe shame over something you already did.
Maybe you have spent years blaming your darkness on the people who wounded you because admitting what has grown inside your own heart feels unbearable.
The Gospel is not Jesus discovering your secret and walking away disgusted.
The Gospel is Jesus knowing the truth and calling you out of hiding.
You cannot shock the Savior who carried the sins of His people to Calvary.
But neither can you follow Him faithfully while demanding permission to keep cherishing what He calls you to surrender.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace brings us to the One who forgives and transforms.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Show me what I keep blaming on everybody else.
Expose what I have learned to excuse.
Teach me to hate what destroys communion with You and love what pleases You.
Create in me a clean heart.
And perhaps someone reading this has never truly trusted Christ at all.
But Christianity is not ultimately the project of making your exterior religious enough to compensate for what is inside.
The crucified and risen Christ calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Not the version your family thinks exists.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
God does not merely address what comes out of us.
Repentance becomes a way of life.
Purity goes to war against lust.
Love begins occupying territory hatred once controlled.
Sometimes involving tears, confession, accountability, restitution, and getting back up after another battle.
But Christ does not merely repaint tombs.
Stay in front of the mirror.
What has been coming out of your heart lately?
When nobody can see your screen?
Run with the answer to Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every private detail. But perhaps you need to stop pretending.
Sometimes two honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Someone quietly drowning beneath religious appearances may encounter it because you refused to keep the Gospel to yourself.
Not because an article can change your heart.
We want this community to remain a place where sinners are not entertained into spiritual sleep but lovingly pointed toward Jesus Christ.
You cannot buy grace. You cannot purchase salvation.

But if this ministry genuinely glorifies Christ, strengthens believers, reaches people with biblical truth, and places Gospel-centered resources into hands that need them, financial support is one practical way believers can participate in keeping that work moving.
The deepest human problem was never merely what surrounded us.
It was what lived within us.
And the breathtaking hope of the Gospel is that Jesus did not stand outside our darkness shouting instructions about how to escape.
He bore sin at the cross.
And He calls sinners out of hiding and into grace.
The heart you are most afraid for Jesus to see may become the very place where His grace writes its most beautiful testimony.
